routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more reasonable than skeptical atheism through a cumulative case from cosmic origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and direct religious experience, while addressing proposed defeaters.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal evidential strands jointly support a personal, morally perfect creator and the Christian identification of that creator more strongly than the skeptical alternatives undermine those inferences.

motionBridge.description: The combined evidence must make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: A beginning of the universe and an applicable causal principle must support a transcendent personal creator.
Life-permitting fine-tuning must favor intelligent design over necessity, chance, or selection-based alternatives.
Objective moral values and duties must require and receive an adequate foundation in God.
Resurrection evidence and religious experience must connect generic theism to the Christian-God hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential strands must be assessed cumulatively under a burden that also requires justification for skeptical atheism.
Objections from evil, hiddenness, religious diversity, and naturalistic epistemology must not defeat the cumulative inference.

routes.description: Show that the specific Christian-God hypothesis lacks sufficient evidential support because its main arguments rely on disputed premises, exceed their conclusions, face natural alternatives, and conflict with evil and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence does not adequately distinguish Christian theism from rival explanations and the observed world supplies material counterevidence to the claimed divine attributes.

motionBridge.description: The evidence must fail to make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Neither an absolute cosmic beginning nor a causal inference to an immaterial personal creator must be treated as established.
Fine-tuning and morality must admit alternatives that prevent their use as distinctive evidence for the Christian God.
Resurrection reports and religious experience must lack the reliability needed to distinguish Christianity from natural or rival religious accounts.
Evil, suffering, and sincere nonbelief must count against a perfectly good, omnipotent, relational God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Christian theism must bear an appropriately demanding burden as one specific supernatural hypothesis among incompatible alternatives.
Any limited anomaly or unexplained cause must not be extended beyond the evidence to the full divine attributes.

sections.title: Burden, Religious Diversity, and Epistemic Method
sections.rationale: This issue governs how the specific Christian hypothesis is compared with skeptical atheism, rival religions, experiential claims, rational intuition, and empirically grounded inquiry.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal inference from the universe's alleged beginning through causal premises to a timeless, immaterial, personal cause.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether life-permitting conditions favor intelligent design and whether that inference reaches the kind of God specified by the motion.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether objective value and obligation exist, whether non-theistic accounts can ground them, and whether a divine lawgiver is required.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on the transition from generic theism to Christianity through historical claims about Jesus and purported immediate awareness of God.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, and Divine Hiddenness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether suffering and sincere nonbelief conflict with the claimed divine attributes and whether the proposed theistic purposes answer that conflict.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe began to exist and therefore has an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, personal cause beyond space and time.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening address presents this as his first argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the principal cosmological route from a beginning and causal premise to a transcendent personal cause.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops an indispensable central bridge with an explicit argument structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is recoverable, but the transition among universe, transcendent cause, and personal being compresses material scope and attribute qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Necessity follows conditionally from the stated premises, but the evidence excerpt does not warrant comparable certainty about every attributed feature or the premises themselves.

charity.alternative: A nonpersonal or differently constituted transcendent cause
charity.decisiveQualification: The cause-to-personal-agent bridge requires more than timelessness and immateriality

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core syllogism is valid conditionally, but the inference from a transcendent cause to a personal being leaves a material bridge underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies an organized causal case, yet the excerpt does not establish the cosmic-beginning premise or compare serious rival causal models sufficiently.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable cosmological-creator bridge and sits at the top of the central-contact tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions constraints on the cause but does not fully answer the strongest nonpersonal-cause alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states that the universe began, infers a transcendent cause, and attributes uncaused, timeless, changeless, immaterial features while invoking an infinite-regress objection.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe's narrowly life-permitting constants and initial conditions are better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this as his second argument during the same uninterrupted opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops the design strand by contrasting physical necessity, chance, and intelligent design.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely develops a central route and expressly identifies the rival explanatory categories.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative design proposition is clear, but the asserted three-option scope and probability basis require qualifications not made explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument presses design strongly while the excerpt leaves probability measures, exhaustive alternatives, and selection effects materially unresolved.

charity.alternative: Chance, necessity, or a selection-based natural explanation
charity.decisiveQualification: Design must be favored under defensible comparative probabilities rather than merely remain possible

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory inference is intelligible, but the exhaustive trilemma and move from improbability to design retain substantial unsupported conditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Narrow life-permitting ranges are invoked, but representative probability support and sustained comparison with selection-based rivals are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the affirmative route's indispensable fine-tuning-to-designer step and therefore ranks highly within central contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move names necessity and chance but treats the option set and comparative probabilities too quickly to resolve the strongest alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls fine-tuning extraordinary, identifies necessity, chance, and design, rejects necessity through independence from laws, and begins a probability objection to chance.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, and their validity and binding force require God as an adequate foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly announces a third argument and develops both premises and its conclusion in his opening speech.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the moral route by asserting objective values and duties and making God their necessary foundation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the central conditional and defines objective values as valid and binding.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional is recoverable, but values, duties, validity, binding force, and grounding are not kept sufficiently distinct for the decisive inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim exceeds the excerpt's support because rival accounts of value and obligation are not yet excluded.

charity.alternative: Objective moral realism without ontological dependence on God
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must show why objectivity or obligation specifically requires a divine foundation

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modus-tollens structure can be recovered, but the major premise contains the principal disputed grounding bridge rather than defending it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt defines objectivity and asserts divine dependence, but supplies little evidence or alternative comparison for that fact-dependent metaphysical premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable divine-grounding bridge and is therefore near the top of central burden contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states divine dependence but does not yet engage the strongest non-theistic realist account of objective value or duty.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt announces the third argument, asks how a creator's goodness can be known, and states that without God objective moral values and duties would not exist.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus' empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' resulting belief are best explained by his resurrection, which entails God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies this as his fourth argument and presents it continuously as part of his enumerated opening case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the principal historical bridge from asserted facts about Jesus to resurrection and Christian identification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances the key route from generic theism to the specifically Christian hypothesis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-fact inference is clear, but majority recognition, historical fact status, best explanation, and divine entailment need material qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The best-explanation claim is pressed strongly without uncertainty about source dependence, base rates, rival explanations, or the precise consensus.

charity.alternative: Natural or legendary explanations of the empty-tomb and appearance traditions
charity.decisiveQualification: A resurrection inference requires comparative historical assessment rather than mere enumeration of asserted facts

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive form is coherent, but the bridge from three asserted facts to a divine resurrection is materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific historical claims and an appeal to historians are offered, but documentation, independence, and serious rival comparison remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable Christian-identification bridge and thus occupies the top of the central-contact band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move organizes affirmative facts but the excerpt does not seriously compare the strongest natural, testimonial, or legendary alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes three allegedly widely recognized facts, begins with the empty tomb, and claims that resurrection best explains them.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A person can know that God exists through immediate personal experience independently of propositional arguments.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces this as his fifth consideration in the uninterrupted conclusion of his opening case.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers immediate experience as an independent epistemic strand within the cumulative method.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it adds a clear experiential consideration but supplies only limited public verification or discrimination.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable, but immediate experience, knowledge, and identification of the experienced reality as God are insufficiently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modal claim is restrained, though its presentation as knowledge omits a material qualification concerning reliability and rival interpretations.

charity.alternative: A psychologically real experience that does not veridically disclose God
charity.decisiveQualification: Phenomenal immediacy alone does not establish the external identity or reliability of its apparent object

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possibility of noninferential knowledge is coherent, but the move leaves the experience-to-veridical-God identification substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt relies on reported biblical experience and an authority's description without representative reliability evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the cumulative epistemic method, but it does not by itself complete the central Christian-identification requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move describes immediate awareness but does not engage the strongest distinction between sincere experience and veridical knowledge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says this is not an argument, claims God can be known wholly apart from arguments, and illustrates the claim through biblical experience and John Hick's description.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Conflicting religions produced through human cognitive tendencies and cultural transmission show that common religious belief-forming methods are unreliable guides to truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican delivers the entire passage continuously in his opening address and expressly distinguishes it from a genetic fallacy.

response.rationale: This constructive move attacks the reliability of religious belief formation by appealing to incompatible outputs and cultural-cognitive production.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a material reliability challenge using the concrete phenomenon of conflicting exclusive religions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is clear, though method, religious experience, and reliability risk overgeneralization across distinct belief-forming practices.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Conflict supports a reliability concern, but incompatibility alone does not show that every relevant method or resulting belief is probably false.

charity.alternative: One religious tradition is true despite widespread incompatible error
charity.decisiveQualification: Diversity undermines an undiscriminating method but does not directly falsify every tradition-specific evidential case

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from systematically conflicting outputs to reduced method reliability is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning heterogeneous methods.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete incompatible religions support the premise, though evidence for the alleged common cognitive and transmission mechanisms is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central challenge to religious-experience reliability, though it is less specific to resurrection testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges that at most one exclusive religion could be true, preserving the strongest qualification while sustaining its method-level criticism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that a method producing conflicting beliefs cannot simply be relied upon and cites Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as mutually exclusive examples.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Because Christianity is one specific hypothesis among numerous incompatible religions and disembodied minds lack solid evidence, it requires an exceptionally strong evidential case.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican states the burden conclusion in his own opening speech and supports it through a continuous comparison with rival hypotheses.

components.text: Whether immediate religious experience can justify the specifically Christian God hypothesis.
Whether the specifically Christian historical hypothesis receives sufficiently discriminating evidence.

response.rationale: The move contacts the need for specifically Christian justification by comparing Christianity with incompatible religions, but its numerical prior-sharing illustration does not fully answer either evidential strand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that reaches the decisive specificity demand while leaving the underlying resurrection and experiential evidence largely unexamined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden conclusion is clear, but the probability allocation across thousands of religions is materially underqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A demanding comparative burden is warranted, but an overwhelming-evidence threshold and equal sharing of prior probability are not established.

charity.alternative: Christianity could possess evidence that distinguishes it from rival religions
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiplicity affects priors only alongside substantive comparison of the rival hypotheses and their evidence

logicalCoherence.rationale: The specificity concern is coherent, but the equal-probability division and inference from insufficient proof to atheism leave substantial gaps.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious multiplicity supports caution, while the numerical prior allocation and claim about disembodied minds lack defended evidential warrants here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary specific-hypothesis burden and stands high within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes that a strong case could prevail but understates how unequal evidence and priors may distinguish the alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt treats Christianity as one claim among thousands, invokes a very strong burden, and says failure of an overwhelming case implies at least agnosticism and perhaps atheism.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Neither the beginning of the local universe nor the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes that the global physical universe had an absolute beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person rebuttal remains within Millican's identified speech and directly addresses Craig by name.

components.text: Whether the evidence establishes an absolute beginning of the global physical universe.
Whether actual infinities and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem rule out an infinite global past.

response.rationale: The move directly distinguishes local from global beginnings and challenges both the infinity and physical-theorem supports for the affirmative premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive beginning premise and identifies why the cited routes do not establish the global conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The local-versus-global distinction and limited theorem conclusion are stated with stable scope and an express qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues underdetermination rather than certainty and appropriately limits its conclusion to what the cited considerations establish.

charity.alternative: The global universe also had a finite past despite the theorem's formal limitation
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure of this theorem to prove a global beginning does not prove an infinite global past

logicalCoherence.rationale: The local-global distinction directly defeats an overbroad inference, with only bounded dependence on the characterization of the theorem.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names the physical theorem and relevant limitation, though the excerpt supplies limited technical documentation of that interpretation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable cosmological-underdetermination bridge and ranks at the top of central contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the modal distinction and attacks establishment rather than claiming that an infinite past has been demonstrated.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly permits an infinite global universe despite a local beginning and identifies actual-infinity arguments and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem as Craig's two supports.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even if the physical universe had a nonphysical cause, identifying it as an immaterial personal mind exceeds both the available evidence and human cognitive competence.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly introduces Craig's further inference and develops the objection continuously in his own speech.

components.text: Whether a nonphysical cause may validly be identified as an immaterial personal mind.

response.rationale: The move diagnoses the missing evidential bridge from nonphysical cause to mind and states the defeating consequence that the personal-cause conclusion remains speculative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies the decisive inference gap and explains why the conclusion exceeds the evidence supplied.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion concerns evidential insufficiency, and the terms mind, physical substrate, and nonphysical cause remain stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the identification speculative is supported, although saying there is no evidence whatever is somewhat stronger than the excerpt establishes.

charity.alternative: A timeless origin is better modeled as agent causation than as a mechanistic condition
charity.decisiveQualification: That conceptual argument still requires support for a substrate-independent mind

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move cogently separates a nonphysical cause from a personal mind and identifies the missing inference without self-undermining.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The absence of demonstrated substrate-independent minds is relevant evidence, though the universal no-evidence claim and cognitive limits are not extensively documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports central cosmological underdetermination by attacking the personal-cause identification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism fairly targets the evidential bridge, though it does not fully examine the strongest conceptual argument for agent causation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly challenges the move from a physical universe's cause to an immaterial mind and cites the lack of evidence for minds without physical substrates.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: A moral argument for God must precisely define the relevant sense of objective value and establish both that such values exist and that they require God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies Craig's moral argument, quotes its definition, and closes his speech by presenting a direct challenge.

components.text: Whether a precise kind of objective value both exists and specifically requires God.
Whether evidence for objectivity uses the same sense required by the divine-grounding premise.

response.rationale: The move directly isolates the two decisive burdens—existence and divine dependence—and demands semantic consistency between them.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both central components explicitly, though it primarily sets a challenge rather than supplying a full alternative account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge clearly distinguishes defining the relevant objectivity from proving its existence and its dependence on God.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expresses doubt rather than certainty and appropriately leaves the challenge open pending the affirmative explanation.

charity.alternative: The affirmative may define objectivity and then defend both premises consistently
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge does not itself show that no such coherent defense is available

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move cleanly separates definition, existence, and divine-dependence requirements without treating any one as automatically settling the others.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: As a burden diagnosis it needs limited external evidence, though its expressed pessimism is not independently supported in this excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable divine-grounding bridge at both of its principal premises.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly says the challenge may be answered and reserves its conclusion until hearing the proposed account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt demands a precise sense of objective morality that requires God and solid evidence that objective values exist in that same sense.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A negative answer to whether God exists requires justification rather than receiving default status, and the case for theism may draw on logic, evidence, and experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig, after which Craig recapitulates his two contentions and directly answers Millican's opening objections.

components.text: Whether only the affirmative bears a justificatory burden in answering the debate question.
Whether skeptical atheism receives default status from religious disagreement alone.

response.rationale: The move contacts unilateral burden allocation by distinguishing atheism from agnosticism, but it does not answer the diversity-based reliability objection or the stronger burden for a specific hypothesis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that contacts the primary burden component while leaving the comparative specificity argument substantially intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The atheism-agnosticism distinction is clear, but the move treats every negative answer as if it asserted a comparably substantive contrary thesis.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Positive atheism requires justification, but the burden symmetry claimed is too broad where the opposing stance is merely withholding belief.

charity.alternative: Skeptical atheism may withhold belief rather than assert God's nonexistence
charity.decisiveQualification: Only a substantive negative conclusion incurs the positive burden identified by the reply

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between defended atheism and default agnosticism is useful, but the burden inference depends on an unresolved characterization of the negative position.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden point is principally conceptual and reasonably supported, though it does not establish symmetry with the specific Christian claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary cumulative-burden method but does not itself complete any substantive evidential strand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move distinguishes agnosticism but does not fully accommodate nonbelief framed as evidential withholding rather than a categorical denial.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt disputes a unilateral burden, frames the motion as a question, and says a negative answer needs justification or else agnosticism remains the default.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Something cannot begin without either a material or an efficient cause, and events in a structured quantum vacuum are not counterexamples to that causal principle.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig directly attributes the contrary objections to Millican and answers them continuously with causal distinctions, quantum physics, and metaphysical reasoning.

components.text: Whether causal counterexamples undermine an efficient-cause requirement for an absolute beginning.
Whether quantum-vacuum events constitute beginnings from literal nothing.

response.rationale: The move directly defends efficient causation and distinguishes structured quantum conditions from literal nothing, but it does not establish that the global universe began.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the causal component fully but only partially answers a move whose decisive global-beginning component remains untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: Material and efficient causes are distinguished clearly, though the universal causal scope is not explicitly limited or defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Distinguishing a quantum vacuum from nothing is sound, but absolute impossibility of an uncaused beginning is asserted beyond the support shown.

charity.alternative: An absolute beginning may not instantiate ordinary intra-universe causal regularities
charity.decisiveQualification: Quantum-vacuum examples fail as creation from nothing, but that does not establish universal causation

logicalCoherence.rationale: The material-versus-efficient distinction is coherent, but the move from experiential absence to metaphysical impossibility leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The structured-vacuum distinction has evidential force, while the universal causal principle is supported mainly by intuition and assertion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks central cosmological underdetermination on causation, though not on the separate global-beginning premise.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly corrects the quantum-vacuum analogy while leaving the strongest domain-applicability challenge unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes absence of a material cause from absence of an efficient cause and argues that lacking both would be still more problematic.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Naturalistic ethical systems do not adequately ground intrinsic human value or binding duties, whereas moral prescriptions are plausibly grounded in a divine lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig marks the transition to the moral argument and directly evaluates the secular ethical theories Millican had previously offered.

components.text: Whether binding moral prescriptions require a personal prescriber or lawgiver.
Whether objective moral values and duties actually exist in the required sense.

response.rationale: The move contacts the divine-dependence component through a prescriber analogy but leaves the independently demanded existence and precise-definition component unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that reaches a decisive grounding component while omitting another decisive component expressly raised by the target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The lawgiver inference is recoverable, but prescription, obligation, command, and objective value are treated as closer equivalents than established.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling divine grounding most plausible exceeds the excerpt's comparison because non-command accounts of reasons and obligations are not addressed.

charity.alternative: Objective obligations are stance-independent reasons rather than commands requiring a commander
charity.decisiveQualification: The linguistic prescriber analogy does not by itself settle the ontology of moral obligation

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if all obligations are prescriptions in a command-like sense, which is the central unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt relies heavily on a prescriber analogy and unspecified expert recognition without substantive comparison with naturalistic moral theories.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central natural-theology-alternatives bridge by defending divine moral grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats prescriptions as necessarily personal commands and omits the strongest impersonal-reasons alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says prescriptions require prescribers, moral prescriptions require a moral prescriber, and obligation is unintelligible without a moral lawgiver.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning supplies at most a cautious design consideration and does not establish the morally perfect, omnipotent Christian God rather than natural alternatives or rival designers.
moves.attributionBasis: Following his introduction by the moderator, Millican explicitly begins his fine-tuning response and sustains it until announcing a new topic.

components.text: Whether fine-tuning favors the specific Christian God over natural or rival designer hypotheses.
Whether current probability and physics claims warrant a confident design inference.
Whether morally perfect rather than evil agency is distinguished by the evidence.

response.rationale: The move contacts the comparative inference, its physical uncertainty, and the attribute gap by presenting natural alternatives and a rival evil designer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts multiple decisive components, including the inference's force and its failure to identify the morally perfect Christian God.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully limited to cautious support and distinguishes generic design from the full Christian-God hypothesis.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move allows fine-tuning some evidential force while calibrating that force to unresolved physics and underdetermination.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning is evidence for a designer even if it does not establish every divine attribute
charity.decisiveQualification: Limited designer evidence may contribute cumulatively without independently proving Christianity

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between generic design evidence and identification of a morally perfect Christian God is clear and inferentially sound.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers several substantive rival considerations, though the excerpt does not fully document their physics or comparative likelihoods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge requiring alternatives to block distinctive fine-tuning evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly concedes cautious design support, though it gives limited attention to its possible cumulative role.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt urges caution about future physics and argues that fine-tuning fails to distinguish a morally perfect God from an equally powerful evil designer.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness does not establish atheism because greater evidence of God's existence might not bring more people freely into a saving relationship with God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig immediately before this uninterrupted first-person rebuttal, and the following transition remains within his speech.

components.text: Whether imperfectly discriminating evidence is compatible with God's purpose of freely formed saving relationships.
Whether God should provide stronger publicly discriminating evidence for the Christian hypothesis.

response.rationale: The reply gives a purpose-based explanation for limited evidence, but it does not directly answer fine-tuning's rival-designer problem and only indirectly contacts the earlier specificity burden.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary evidence-level issue but not the primary fine-tuning inference, making it a limited partial answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is explicitly modal and consistently concerns whether additional evidence would improve saving relationships.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The repeated 'may' and 'perhaps' language appropriately presents a possible compatibility explanation rather than an established fact.

charity.alternative: Sincere seekers might freely respond if stronger evidence were available
charity.decisiveQualification: A bare possibility about divine foreknowledge does not establish that all nonbelief is resistant

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility response is coherent, but it depends on a speculative counterfactual about evidence and free saving response.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No representative evidence is supplied for the claim that stronger evidence would do no more relational good.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central evil-hiddenness counterevidence bridge, although its contact with the selected earlier move is indirect.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a coherent theistic possibility but insufficiently addresses sincere nonresistant nonbelief.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God's aim is saving relationship and speculates that more evidence might not bring additional people into such a relationship.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The narrow life-permitting range and multiple independent instances of cosmic fine-tuning remain evidence for design despite objections about probability, unsettled physics, efficiency, and cosmic scale.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces the fine-tuning argument and sequentially answers the numbered objections attributed to Millican throughout the same speech.

components.text: Whether fine-tuning remains design evidence despite probability and unsettled-physics objections.
Whether the life-permitting range is sufficiently narrow to sustain the likelihood comparison.
Whether fine-tuning identifies the Christian God rather than rival designers.

response.rationale: The reply answers several probability and physical-range objections but leaves the decisive attribute and rival-designer underdetermination substantially unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer contacting the primary evidential component while omitting the specific-God component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The defense is clear, though counting several independent instances and comparing possible ranges require scope and measure qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges caution but treats range comparison as more straightforward than the unresolved measure and theory issues warrant.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning probabilities are ill-defined and generic design does not identify the Christian God
charity.decisiveQualification: Narrow ranges may answer one objection while leaving measure choice and designer identity unresolved

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply coherently explains why narrow ranges are relevant, but probability measures and designer identity remain material bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It cites multiple instances and narrow life-permitting ranges, yet their independence, measures, and full rival comparison remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central natural-theology-alternatives bridge on the fine-tuning strand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply takes several objections in turn but does not fully preserve the strongest underdetermination and probability qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly enumerates Millican's objections, accepts caution, rejects the probability objection, and appeals to comparison between possible and life-permitting ranges.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Atheists can affirm intrinsic human worth and objective moral values without treating those values as ontologically dependent on God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican begins this moral discussion within his introduced final rebuttal, cites survey figures, and directly challenges positions he attributes to Craig.

components.text: Whether objective value and intrinsic human worth can be affirmed without a divine lawgiver.
Whether objective moral values ontologically depend upon God's existence.

response.rationale: The move directly denies that atheism precludes objective value or intrinsic worth, but it offers less explanation of how binding duties are grounded.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive dependence claim but remains a partial answer because a developed non-theistic grounding account is absent.

precisionFindings.rationale: The denial of dependence is clear, but objective value, intrinsic worth, perception, and obligation are not fully separated.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The Gospel resurrection narratives provide weak evidence for divine resurrection because they are late, dependent, partisan, discrepant, and unsupported by contemporary sources.

components.text: Whether the Gospel evidence reliably establishes the facts used in the resurrection inference.

response.rationale: The move diagnoses source lateness, dependence, partisanship, discrepancies, and missing contemporary corroboration, with the consequence that the resurrection inference lacks a reliable factual base.

moves.proposition: Religious experiences and resurrection reports require psychological and natural investigation because comparable supernatural claims arise in mutually incompatible traditions.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The world's evil is empirical evidence against a perfectly good God, while limited supernatural evidence would not establish an omnipotent and omniscient deity.
moves.attributionBasis: Millican announces the problem of evil, anticipates Craig's response, and carries the argument through the explicit conclusion of his closing speech.

components.text: Whether the observed world discriminates a perfectly good God from rival supernatural agents.
Whether limited design evidence establishes omnipotence, omniscience, or perfect goodness.
